messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Farmer
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Certain Songs: Certain songs
  Maladaptive Strategies: Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Sleep: Going to sleep or lying in the dark
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Vinh

Vinh was forty-two when his daughter Linh stopped breathing. She was seven. It happened on an ordinary Tuesday evening in late September, three years ago, when she complained of a headache and a burning throat. By midnight, her fever had spiked to 104, and her small body had begun to convulse. Vinh's wife called 911 while he held Linh's rigid frame, watching her eyes roll back, unable to do anything but feel the heat radiating from her skin and hear the terrible, wet sound of her struggling for air. At the hospital, the diagnosis came swiftly: bacterial meningitis. For six hours, while Linh lay sedated in the pediatric ICU, Vinh sat in a vinyl chair outside her room, watching through the observation window as nurses in full protective gear moved around her small body—the pale, mottled skin of her arms and legs visible beneath the monitors and IV lines, her chest rising and falling with the ventilator's rhythm. She survived, eventually. But something in Vinh did not.

In the months that followed, sleep became impossible. Vinh found that the moment darkness fell, his mind would flood with fragments of that night—not the whole sequence, but pieces that arrived without warning. The sight of Linh's arm, limp against the hospital sheet. The sound of the monitor's beeping. The particular gray-blue color of her fingernails when her oxygen had been dropping. These fragments would flash across his consciousness like lightning, vivid and immediate, and he would be back in that room, his daughter dying in front of him, even though he knew intellectually that she was downstairs in her bedroom, safe and sleeping. The memory did not feel like something that had happened and passed; it felt like something happening now, in the present moment, as real as his own breathing.

Vinh began to stay awake. He told himself it was just until he felt calm enough to lie down, but the hours stretched. He would sit in the living room with the television on low, or work on his laptop, or walk the perimeter of his small farm in the pre-dawn darkness—anything to keep moving, to keep the fragments at bay. But the avoidance only seemed to sharpen his vigilance. Every night, as the sun set and the light drained from the sky, his body would tense. Nighttime itself had become a trigger. Lying in the dark felt like stepping back into that hospital room, and he could not do it. When his wife finally insisted he try to sleep, he would lie beside her for a few minutes, feel the darkness pressing down, and then slip out of bed to sit in the kitchen with all the lights on.

Certain details had become unbearable. When his daughter wore short sleeves, the sight of her small arms—the same size, the same shape as they had been in the hospital—would send him spiraling. He would look away, or excuse himself from the room. A song came on the radio one morning, something that had been playing in the hospital waiting room, and hearing it again made his heart race so violently that he had to pull his truck over. Now he avoided that song, and then others that sounded similar, and eventually he found himself avoiding music altogether, keeping the radio off, the house quiet. These triggers—the sight of her bare skin, the darkness of night, an unexpected melody—would pull the memory forward again, making it feel present and urgent, and each time the memory surfaced, he would feel the panic building, would feel the need to do something, anything, to escape the sensation of being back there.

His avoidance had metastasized into isolation. He began to withdraw from neighbors and friends. He would not attend his nephew's wedding because it was in the evening, and he could not face the drive home in darkness. He stopped going to the weekly gatherings at his church. He told himself he was protecting his family from his own instability, but the truth was more complicated: being around other people meant being asked questions, meant having to manage his expression, meant being in situations where he could not control the light or the sounds or the unexpected triggers that might pull him back into that room. His wife noticed his withdrawal, and it created a distance between them that had not been there before. His farm work suffered too. During the day, he could manage, but as harvest season approached and the days grew shorter, he found himself exhausted and unable to concentrate, his mind caught in a loop of avoidance and dread.

The fragments came more frequently now, and they came in response to his own attempts to avoid them. The harder he fought against sleep, the more vivid the intrusions became. The longer he stayed awake, the more fragmented and surreal his thinking grew, and the more desperate he became to find new ways to escape. He had come to believe that sleep itself was dangerous, that if he closed his eyes in the dark, something catastrophic would happen—not just to him, but to his daughter, as if his vigilance was the only thing keeping her alive. Three years into this cycle, Vinh was hollow-eyed and desperate. He had lost fifteen pounds. His marriage was strained to the breaking point. It was only when his wife threatened to leave, to take Linh away because she could not watch him disappear, that he finally made an appointment with a therapist. He sat in the waiting room, terrified that talking about what had happened would only make it more real, more present. But he was more terrified of losing his family. He needed to understand why the night would not let him go, and why his own mind had become his enemy.
